Insights / Search & discovery

A practical technical SEO checklist for small business websites

Before publishing more pages, check whether the pages you already have can be found and understood. Technical SEO is not a collection of tricks. It is the work of removing avoidable barriers between your website, search engines, and the people looking for your business.

By Shahir Salehi3 minute readPractical guide

In this guide

  1. Start with the pages that matter
  2. Check the response before the metadata
  3. Review indexing instructions together
  4. Follow the internal links
  5. Read the rendered HTML
  6. Test mobile usability and loading
  7. Turn findings into a release plan

Start with the pages that matter

List the pages that explain your core offering and provide a useful next step. For a service business, that may be the homepage, a few service pages, and contact information. For a store, include representative categories and products. This list gives the review a business purpose. A warning affecting an unused filter URL should not automatically outrank a missing service page.

Check the response before the metadata

Open each priority URL directly. It should load the intended page without requiring a visit to the homepage first. Check for redirect loops, unnecessary chains, and pages that display an error while returning a successful HTTP response. A removed page should have a relevant replacement or a real 404 response; redirecting every missing URL to the homepage makes errors harder to interpret.

Review indexing instructions together

Robots.txt controls crawler access, while a noindex directive asks supported search engines not to index a page. They are not substitutes for access control. A canonical tag indicates the preferred URL for substantially equivalent content; it does not guarantee that the engine will choose it. Review these signals together with the XML sitemap. A page intended for indexing should not be blocked, marked noindex, and listed in the sitemap at the same time.

Follow the internal links

Important pages need links from other useful pages. A sitemap helps discovery but does not replace navigation. Check that service pages appear in the services hub, that relevant articles link to them, and that breadcrumbs lead to real parent pages. Use descriptive anchors that explain the destination. Avoid creating long lists of repeated keyword links that make the page harder to read.

Read the rendered HTML

The main heading and page content should be present in the generated HTML, particularly on a content-led site. Check titles, descriptions, and headings on representative templates. One useful H1 is easier to maintain than several competing page titles. Structured data should describe facts visible on the page; adding a schema type does not create a qualification, review, or ranking entitlement.

Test mobile usability and loading

Use a narrow viewport and keyboard navigation. Look for clipped menus, horizontal scrolling, hard-to-use forms, and layout shifts caused by assets without dimensions. Review large images and unnecessary scripts before reaching for complex optimization. Lab measurements help diagnose a problem; real-user data, when available, helps show whether it affects visitors. Neither should be replaced with an invented performance score.

Turn findings into a release plan

Record the URL, observed behavior, expected behavior, business impact, proposed correction, and owner. Test one representative template before a broad rollout. After publishing, recheck the live response, canonical, internal links, and sitemap. Search Console can then help monitor discovery and indexing, but a request for indexing does not guarantee an immediate result.

Put it into practice

  • Priority URLs load directly and return the expected status.
  • Indexing signals and sitemap entries agree.
  • Navigation and internal links reach every important page.
  • Templates contain useful HTML content and factual structured data.
  • Mobile journeys work, and published corrections have been rechecked.
